items.stem: The order of rotational symmetry of a shape is
options: the number of lines of symmetry
the number of times it fits onto itself in one full turn
items.answer: the number of times it fits onto itself in one full turn
items.markingKey: Count the positions in 360° where the shape looks the same.

items.stem: Explain why a diagonal of a rectangle (not a square) is not a line of symmetry.
items.answer: Reflecting in a diagonal would swap the long and short sides, so the image would not fit exactly onto the rectangle.
items.markingKey: B1 reflection swaps sides; B1 sides unequal [2]

items.stem: Explain why a parallelogram has rotational symmetry but no line symmetry.
items.answer: A half turn about the centre maps it onto itself, but folding along any line does not match the slanting sides exactly.
items.markingKey: B1 half turn; B1 no fold line matches [2]

items.stem: A regular decagon is rotated about its centre. Write down its order of rotational symmetry and calculate the smallest angle of rotation that maps it onto itself.
items.answer: Order 10; 36°

items.stem: The smallest angle of rotation that maps a regular polygon onto itself is 60°. Find the number of sides, the number of lines of symmetry and the size of one interior angle.
items.answer: 6 sides; 6 lines of symmetry; interior angle 120°

items.stem: A logo for a company in Manila is a regular octagon of side 4 cm. (a) Write down the number of lines of symmetry. (b) Write down the order of rotational symmetry. (c) Calculate the area of the logo.
A shape with rotational symmetry of order 1
items.answer: has no rotational symmetry
items.markingKey: Every shape fits onto itself once in a full turn (the starting position).

items.stem: Explain why every regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.
items.answer: All sides and angles are equal, so there is a line through each vertex or side-midpoint and the centre, and rotating by 360°/n maps it onto itself n times.
items.markingKey: B1 lines through centre; B1 rotation by 360°/n [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between line symmetry and rotational symmetry.
items.answer: Line symmetry: the shape folds onto itself along a mirror line. Rotational symmetry: the shape fits onto itself when turned about a centre point less than a full turn.
items.markingKey: B1 line description; B1 rotation description [2]

items.stem: Felix says an isosceles triangle and a capital letter H have exactly the same symmetry. Explain whether Felix is correct, stating the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of each.
items.answer: Not correct: isosceles triangle: 1 line, order 1; capital letter H: 2 lines, order 2.
items.markingKey: B1 each shape correct; B1 conclusion [3]

items.stem: A shape has the line x = 0 as a line of symmetry. Two of its vertices are (−4, −3) and (−2, 5). Write down the coordinates of the two vertices that are their images in this line.
items.markingKey: B1 B1 (each point is the same distance from x = 0 on the other side).

items.stem: A regular nonagon is rotated about its centre. Write down its order of rotational symmetry and calculate the smallest angle of rotation that maps it onto itself.
items.answer: Order 9; 40°

items.stem: A shape has the line y = 3 as a line of symmetry. Two of its vertices are (0, −2) and (−1, 1). Write down the coordinates of the two vertices that are their images in this line.
items.markingKey: B1 B1 (each point is the same distance from y = 3 on the other side).

items.stem: A logo for a company in Lagos is a regular dodecagon of side 6 cm. (a) Write down the order of rotational symmetry. (b) The logo is rotated clockwise about its centre through 150°. Explain whether it looks the same as before.
items.answer: (a) 12 (b) Yes: it maps onto itself only for multiples of 30°.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 [1] (b) B1 conclusion; B1 reason [2]

items.stem: A logo for a company in Bangkok is a regular octagon of side 5 cm. (a) Write down the number of lines of symmetry. (b) Write down the order of rotational symmetry. (c) Calculate the distance from the centre to the midpoint of one side.
A plane of symmetry divides a 3D shape into
options: two congruent shapes of any orientation
two halves that are mirror images of each other
items.answer: two halves that are mirror images of each other
items.markingKey: The plane acts like a mirror.

items.stem: How many planes of symmetry does a cube have?
items.markingKey: 3 parallel to pairs of faces and 6 through pairs of opposite edges.

items.stem: Explain why a cube has more planes of symmetry than a cuboid with three different edge lengths.
items.answer: All faces of a cube are equal squares, so as well as the 3 planes parallel to faces there are 6 diagonal planes through opposite edges; in the cuboid the diagonal planes do not give mirror images.
items.markingKey: B1 3 face-parallel planes in both; B1 6 extra diagonal planes for cube [2]

items.stem: A right pyramid has a base that is an equilateral triangle, with its apex directly above the centre of the base. Write down (a) the number of planes of symmetry and (b) the order of rotational symmetry about the vertical axis.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 3 planes, each containing the axis and a line of symmetry of the base (b) B1 3.

items.stem: A chocolate box made in Singapore is a right prism of length 15 cm. Its cross-section is a regular hexagon of side 3 cm. (a) Write down the number of planes of symmetry of the box. (b) Calculate the volume of the box.
Explain the difference between a plane of symmetry and an axis of rotational symmetry.
items.answer: A plane of symmetry reflects the solid onto itself; an axis of symmetry is a line about which the solid can be rotated (less than a full turn) to fit onto itself.
items.markingKey: B1 plane = reflection; B1 axis = rotation [2]

items.stem: Grace says that a right prism whose cross-section is a regular polygon with 3 sides has 3 planes of symmetry, the same as the number of lines of symmetry of the cross-section. Explain why Grace is not quite right.
items.answer: There are 3 vertical planes through the lines of symmetry of the cross-section, plus one more plane halfway along the prism parallel to the ends, so 4 planes.
items.markingKey: B1 3 planes from the cross-section; B1 extra plane through the middle, total 4 [2]

items.stem: A right prism has a cross-section that is a regular dodecagon. Write down (a) the number of planes of symmetry and (b) the order of rotational symmetry about the axis through the centres of its two end faces.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 12 planes through the axis and 1 parallel to the ends (b) B1 12.

items.stem: Explain why the perpendicular from the centre O to a chord AB bisects AB.
items.answer: OA = OB (radii), so triangle OAB is isosceles; the perpendicular from O is a line of symmetry, so it meets AB at its midpoint (RHS congruent triangles).
items.markingKey: B1 radii equal/isosceles; B1 symmetry or congruence [2]

items.stem: Explain why the two tangents from an external point to a circle are equal in length.
items.answer: The triangles formed with the centre are right-angled (tangent ⟂ radius), share the hypotenuse OP and have equal radii, so they are congruent (RHS) and the tangents are equal.
items.markingKey: B1 right angles; B1 congruent triangles (RHS) [2]

items.answer: (a) 90°: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. (b) 14.4 cm (c) Triangles OAP and OBP are congruent (RHS), so reflecting in OP maps A to B.

items.stem: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is
options: twice the angle subtended at the circumference
half the angle at the circumference
equal to the angle at the circumference
items.answer: twice the angle subtended at the circumference

items.stem: Explain why the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
items.answer: The diameter subtends an angle of 180° at the centre, and the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre, so it is 90°.
items.markingKey: B1 angle at centre 180°; B1 half is 90° [2]

items.stem: Explain why a quadrilateral with opposite angles of 100° and 70° cannot be cyclic.
items.answer: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral must add up to 180°, but 100° + 70° = 170°.
items.markingKey: B1 rule; B1 check [2]

items.stem: TA is a tangent to a circle at A. B and C are points on the circle. Angle TAB = 63° and C is in the alternate segment. Find angle ACB and angle AOB, where O is the centre, giving reasons.
items.answer: Angle ACB = 63°; angle AOB = 126°
items.markingKey: B1 ACB = 63° (alternate segment theorem); B1 AOB = 126° (angle at centre twice angle at circumference); B1 reasons.

items.stem: A tangent from a point P touches a circle with centre O and radius 12 cm at T. OP = 20 cm. Tariq calculates PT = √(20² + 12²) = 23.3 cm. Explain the error and find PT.
items.answer: Angle OTP = 90°, so OP is the hypotenuse: PT = √(20² − 12²) = 16.0 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 OP is hypotenuse (tangent ⟂ radius); M1 √(20² − 12²); A1 16.0 cm [3]

items.stem: A tangent from a point P touches a circle with centre O and radius 12 cm at T. OP = 15 cm. Yusuf calculates PT = √(15² + 12²) = 19.2 cm. Explain the error and find PT.
items.answer: Angle OTP = 90°, so OP is the hypotenuse: PT = √(15² − 12²) = 9.00 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 OP is hypotenuse (tangent ⟂ radius); M1 √(15² − 12²); A1 9.00 cm [3]

items.stem: A chord of length 8.3 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 5 cm. Calculate the distance of the chord from the centre.
items.markingKey: M1 half-chord 4.15; M1 √(5² − 4.15²); A1 2.79 cm.

items.stem: A circle has centre O and radius 9 cm. The chord AB is 6.2 cm from O. Calculate the length of AB.
items.markingKey: B1 perpendicular from O bisects AB; M1 √(9² − 6.2²) = 6.52; A1 13.0 cm.

items.stem: Tangents PA and PB are drawn from a point P to a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm. OP = 13 cm. (a) Calculate angle APB. (b) Explain why OP is a line of symmetry of OAPB.
items.answer: (a) 45.2° (b) Triangles OAP and OBP are congruent (RHS), so reflecting in OP maps A to B.

items.stem: A, B, C and D lie on a circle, with C and D on the same side of AB. Angle ACB = 59°. Aisha says angle ADB = 121°. Explain the error and give the correct angle.
items.answer: Angles in the same segment are equal, so angle ADB = 59°; 121° would only apply to a point on the other side of AB (cyclic quadrilateral).
items.markingKey: B1 same segment theorem; B1 59° [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the angle in a semicircle is 90°. (b) Give a reason why triangle OAB, where O is the centre and A and B are on the circle, is isosceles.
items.answer: (a) The diameter subtends an angle of 180° at the centre, and the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre, so it is 90°. (b) OA and OB are both radii, so they are equal.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 angle at centre 180°; B1 half is 90° [2] (b) B1 radii equal; B1 base angles equal [2]

items.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle DAB = 67° and angle ABC = 111°. Find angle BCD and angle CDA, giving a reason.
items.answer: Angle BCD = 113°; angle CDA = 69°
items.markingKey: B1 113°; B1 69°; B1 opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

items.stem: A, B and C lie on a circle with centre O. Angle ACB = 28°. Calculate angle OAB, giving reasons for each step.
items.markingKey: B1 angle AOB = 56° (angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference); M1 OA = OB radii so triangle isosceles; A1 (180 − 56) ÷ 2 = 62°.

items.stem: A, B, C and D lie on a circle with centre O. C and D are on opposite sides of the chord AB, with C on the major arc. TA is the tangent at A, on the opposite side of AB from C. Angle ACB = 78°. (a) Find angle OAB, giving reasons. (b) Find angle TAB, giving a reason. (c) Find angle OAT, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) 12°: triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB radii). (b) 78°: alternate segment theorem (or 90° − 12° using tangent ⟂ radius). (c) 90°: tangent is perpendicular to the radius.
